summary: A DHCPv4 server is the authoritative source of the IP addresses it has handed out. Leasequery gives other processes and devices a lightweight way to ask the server about that address information. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: The address clerk keeps a list of who has which address. This lets other devices ask the clerk a quick question about it.

questions: how to query a dhcp server for lease information
how does a relay agent find a client location
subtitle: How a relay agent asks a DHCPv4 server who holds an address, without broadcasting or adding a new protocol.

tldr.problem: An access concentrator that acts as a DHCP relay agent learns where each customer is by watching DHCP traffic, but it loses that knowledge when it reboots or is replaced.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCP message, DHCPLEASEQUERY, lets the relay agent ask a DHCP server about one IP address, MAC address or Client-identifier. The server answers with DHCPLEASEACTIVE, DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED or DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN.
tldr.outcome: The relay agent can rebuild its location information from the authoritative source. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6148.

today: RFC 4388 is a Proposed Standard and is listed as updated by RFC 6148. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: Forgetful Access Concentrators
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 server holds authoritative information about the IP addresses it has leased. Some devices need that information. The main example is the access concentrator, a router or switch at the edge of a broadband access network that also works as a DHCP relay agent.

Such a device normally learns where each host sits by gleaning: it reads the location details out of the DHCP packets it forwards. That knowledge is lost when the device reboots or is replaced. The location matters because it lets the device forward traffic to the right port, virtual circuit and modem, check the source address of incoming datagrams, and encrypt traffic that only the right modem can decrypt.

This RFC adds DHCPLEASEQUERY, a new DHCP message sent from a relay agent to a server, so the device can recover that information. It applies to DHCPv4 only. The RFC says that an equivalent for DHCPv6 would be designing for an imagined consumer.
sections.eli5: A helper at the front desk remembers who is in which room, but forgets everything when it is switched off. The new message lets it ask the person who keeps the master list.

sections.title: Why Not ARP, SNMP or LDAP
sections.content:
The RFC compares leasequery with other ways to find the same information. A broadcast ARP request is undesirable for three reasons: the concentrator must transmit over many ports and virtual circuits, every subscriber host must process the broadcast, and a malicious host can easily pretend to be the endpoint.

Access concentrators typically have no SNMP or LDAP client interfaces. The proposed DHCP Server MIB gives server-wide summaries, while leasequery returns detailed data about individual leases. DHCPLEASEQUERY is also optional for servers, which fits poorly with a MIB.

DHCP servers take part in every lease transaction, so they are the most reliable source. A concentrator can query the same servers its relay agent already uses, and it can be configured with several servers so that none is a single point of failure.
sections.eli5: Shouting the question at the whole street is noisy, and someone might lie. Asking the one person who wrote the list down is quieter and more trustworthy.

sections.title: Three Ways to Ask
sections.content:
The access concentrator starts every conversation. A server that supports the message MUST implement all three query regimes, and must always answer.

  • By IP address: the requester gives only an IP address. The server returns what it knows about the most recent client assigned that address. This form SHOULD be used if possible.
  • By MAC address: the requester gives only a MAC address. The server returns the IP address most recently used by a client with that MAC address, and may list other addresses in different subnets.
  • By Client-identifier: the requester gives only a Client-identifier option (option 61), with similar results.

Servers that do not implement the message SHOULD simply not respond. A server that supports it SHOULD save the most recent Relay Agent Information option (option 82) and the Vendor class identifier (option 60) for each address, since requesters are likely to ask for them.
sections.eli5: You can look someone up by their room number, by their name tag or by their ID card. The clerk can answer any of the three.

sections.title: New Message Types and Options
sections.content:
The message type option (option 53) gets four new values: 10 for DHCPLEASEQUERY, 11 for DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED, 12 for DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN and 13 for DHCPLEASEACTIVE.

Two new options are defined. client-last-transaction-time (code 91, length 4) says how many seconds in the past the client last dealt with the server about this address. It MUST NOT be an absolute time. It is mainly used to compare answers from two servers. associated-ip (code 92) lists all other addresses tied to the client. Its minimum length is 4 octets and the length MUST be a multiple of 4.

IANA assigned these six values.
sections.eli5: The message gets four new names on its label, and two new boxes for notes: one says how long ago the client last visited, and one lists the client's other addresses.

sections.title: Sending the Query and Building the Answer
sections.content:
The query uses the normal DHCP format. The giaddr field MUST be set to the requester's own address. It is only the return address and MUST NOT be used to pick an address pool or restrict the search. A query MUST have a non-zero giaddr and exactly one of: a non-zero ciaddr, a non-zero htype/hlen/chaddr, or a Client-identifier option. If giaddr is zero, the server MUST NOT reply.

The Parameter Request List (option 55) says which options the requester wants, likely the IP Address Lease Time (option 51), Relay Agent Information (option 82) and perhaps option 60.

The server answers in one of three ways. DHCPLEASEACTIVE means there is an active lease, and carries the address in ciaddr, the client's MAC address and the requested options. DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED means the server manages the address but no lease is active, and carries no other options. DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN means the server does not manage the address or knows nothing about the client, and MUST NOT include other options. If several addresses match, the server MUST return the one from the most recent transaction unless an administrator configured another preference.

Servers SHOULD return only options on a configurable list of non-sensitive options.
sections.eli5: You write the question on a card with your own return address. The clerk answers yes, there is a tenant; no, the room is empty; or never heard of it.

sections.title: Caching, Silence and Retries
sections.content:
When the concentrator gets a DHCPLEASEACTIVE answer it SHOULD use the MAC address and Relay Agent Information to refresh its location data. A DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED answer SHOULD be cached, so that a misbehaving device downstream cannot cause excessive load. A DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN answer SHOULD be cached for a short time, approximately 5 minutes.

No answer may mean the message was lost or the server was busy, or that the server does not support leasequery. The two cannot be told apart. The concentrator SHOULD retry with an approximately exponential backoff, aiming at no more than about one packet every 10 seconds to a server not known to support the message and no less than one per 70 seconds. The RFC sketches a per-server timer of one minute, and says the number of parallel queries SHOULD be limited to 100 or 200.

When several servers answer with conflicting data, the client-last-transaction-time can be used to decide which is more recent.
sections.eli5: If the clerk says nobody lives there, write it down so you do not keep asking. If the clerk stays silent, wait a bit longer each time before asking again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Keeping location data accurate helps the concentrator avoid relying on ARP broadcasts, which malicious hosts can exploit. On the other side, the mapping from hardware address to IP lease can invade subscriber privacy, so servers SHOULD protect it with the techniques of RFC 3118, authentication for DHCP messages. The access concentrator is treated as a DHCP client for this purpose.

Denial of service is a concern. Concentrators SHOULD use negative caching and SHOULD NOT send a query for a ciaddr outside the attached broadband networks. Servers SHOULD make sure they cannot be flooded with queries, and may be configured with the relay agents allowed to query them, which the RFC says gives no true security but may thwart unsophisticated attacks.
sections.eli5: The list shows who lives where, so the clerk should only tell trusted helpers, and helpers should not pester the clerk with too many questions.

items.desc: Asks about an IP address, MAC address or Client-identifier.

items.desc: Server manages the address but it has no active lease.

items.desc: Server has no definitive information about the query.
